NVIDIA (NVDA) is a semiconductor company founded in 1993, best known for designing graphics processing units (GPUs) that power gaming, professional visualization, and artificial intelligence.

**What it does:** NVIDIA designs GPUs and the surrounding software ecosystem. Its chips accelerate workloads ranging from real-time graphics to large-scale machine learning. The company's CUDA software platform has become the de facto standard for general-purpose GPU computing. NVIDIA sells into gaming, data centers, professional visualization, and automotive markets.

**Core insight:** NVIDIA's long bet was that parallel computation on GPUs would matter far beyond graphics. That paid off as machine learning came to rely on the massive parallelism GPUs provide, making NVIDIA a central supplier of the hardware behind modern AI. The combination of its chips and the CUDA software moat is core to its market position.

**Market position:** NVIDIA became one of the most valuable companies in the world on the back of demand for AI accelerators, joining the small group of US firms to cross multi-trillion-dollar valuations. Its data-center business now rivals or exceeds its historical gaming roots, and its results are widely watched as a barometer for AI infrastructure spending.

Microsoft's 1986 IPO created one of the largest concentrations of wealth in technology. After a strategic pivot to cloud under new leadership, it returned to the front rank of the industry and is now among the most heavily weighted constituents of the S&P 500.

# Microsoft: Full Picture

**Price:** MSFT is trading at $499.54, up 0.64% today on volume of 526,666 shares.

**What it does:**
Microsoft is a multinational technology company founded in 1975 and one of the largest software and cloud-computing firms in the world. It develops, licenses, and supports software, services, devices, and cloud infrastructure. Its best-known products include the Windows operating system, the Office and Microsoft 365 productivity suite, the Azure cloud platform, the Xbox gaming business, and the LinkedIn professional network.

The company's modern strategy centres on cloud and recurring software revenue—moving customers from one-off licences to subscriptions and consumption-based cloud services. Azure positions Microsoft as one of the dominant providers of cloud infrastructure, whilst deep enterprise relationships give it broad reach across business computing.
